structure.title: By the Ilissus – Socrates’s First Speech · A concealed manuscript changes the afternoon
structure.text: Outside Athens, Phaedrus brings out a speech by Lysias arguing that a young man should favour a suitor who is free of love. Socrates agrees to compete. What looks like a clever exercise gives the pair something consequential to get wrong.

structure.title: The Palinode · A speaker asks to take it back
structure.text: Uneasy about his treatment of love, Socrates delivers a second speech. Images of a winged soul and a charioteer let him explore what a lover might recognise in another person before knowing how to explain it.

structure.title: Rhetoric and the True Art of Speech – On Writing · Two listeners examine what just happened
structure.text: The men compare speeches and ask what training could make persuasion an art. The closing discussion of writing raises a difficulty the manuscript has embodied all afternoon. Its author can neither hear an objection nor choose who gets the next copy.

people.name: Phaedrus
people.text: He can lure Socrates out of town with the promise of a speech. His appetite for fine performances makes him an ideal listener and a test of what listening well actually requires.

people.name: Lysias
people.text: Only his text is present. As the two men test where its parts belong and what its speaker knows, the afternoon gradually exposes the limits of entrusting an argument to a sheet of writing.

context.title: A recantation is a new performance
context.text: Socrates wants to make amends for his first speech by speaking again. Both speeches therefore matter when the men later ask how truth, arrangement and the listener's disposition work together.

notice.text: Keep track of who is reading.
notice.why: The copied speech, an attempted recitation and the conversation under the trees offer different relationships between speaker and audience. The argument about writing has been unfolding in gestures long before it becomes explicit.

notice.text: Listen for changes in what love means.
notice.why: One speech treats desire as an unreliable claimant on a young man's future. Another imagines desire educating the lover. A speech can win an argument simply by choosing what its subject will be allowed to mean.

opening: Phaedrus has found a clever speech arguing that a young man should favour someone who does not love him. Lovers, it explains, are jealous, unreliable, and likely to regret their generosity. Socrates can improve on the performance, but begins to suspect that cleverness has made them speak badly about something they do not understand. A walk outside Athens becomes an argument about desire and persuasion: what happens when someone learns to move another person's soul without first caring what is true.
